Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> Opinion The Quiet Engine of Growth: Why the right legal structure is your Ghanaian MSMEs’ greatest scaling tool Source : Kweku Hammond 18 October 2026 9:56pm Audio By Carbonatix
You started your business to sell a product, deliver a service, or solve a problem you understood better than anyone else. You did not start it to read the Companies Act, 2019 (Act 992), or to decode the finer points of the Ghana Enterprises Agency Act, 2020 (Act 1043). Yet the uncomfortable truth is that some of the most ambitious micro and small enterprises (MSMEs) in Ghana hit a ceiling not because their ideas failed, but because their legal identities could not keep up with their ambition.
Ghana’s MSME sector is the undisputed backbone of the economy. It accounts for over 90 per cent of all businesses and contributes roughly 70 per cent to national GDP. But a vast number still operate as sole proprietorships or informal partnerships, outside the structured regulatory framework that unlocks serious scale. The law does not force you to incorporate. But discretion is not the same as strategy. Here are seven reasons why the legal structure and regulatory classification you choose may be the single most consequential business decision you make, and how each one directly helps a micro or small company scale up.
The most fundamental legal decision is whether your business has a separate legal identity from you. In a sole proprietorship, popularly called a “one-man business”, it does not. You are the business. If a large order goes wrong, if a buyer refuses to pay, or if a contract dispute turns ugly, your personal savings, your family’s home in Kumasi, and your children’s school fees are all on the table. The same is true for a general partnership under the Incorporated Private Partnerships Act, 1962 (Act 152), where Section 16 makes every partner jointly and severally liable for the firm’s debts.
A Private Limited Company under the Companies Act, 2019 (Act 992), changes this. Section 7(2)(a) defines it as a company “which has the liability of its members limited to the amount unpaid on the shares respectively held by them”. The company is a separate legal person. For a micro entrepreneur in Accra or Takoradi, this is not an abstract legal nicety. It is what allows you to take the calculated risks that scaling requires: bidding for a larger contract, entering a new regional market, hiring more people without exposing everything you own. As the Office of the Registrar of Companies (ORC) itself puts it, incorporation “safeguards personal assets from business debts”.
Access to credit is the perennial complaint of the small entrepreneur. The Bank of Ghana has identified a staggering US$4.8 billion annual financing gap for MSMEs, with only about 35 per cent having access to bank financing and over 50 per cent completely shut out of formal credit. But the regulatory and legal framework has changed in your favour if you are positioned to use it.
The Collateral Registry, established under the Borrowers and Lenders Act, 2008 and reinforced by the 2020 Act (Act 1052), was the first of its kind in Africa. It allows MSMEs who lack traditional land or buildings to use movable assets, stock, receivables, vehicles, machinery, and tools of trade to secure credit. Between 2010 and 2025, the Registry recorded over 1.92 million secured transactions. But a sole proprietor operating informally cannot fully leverage this architecture. A registered company or a formalised enterprise with proper documentation is visible to lenders, can register security interests, and can access the venture capital ecosystem that the Venture Capital Trust Fund (VCTF) has built over two decades: 77 companies funded, over GHS 2 billion in leveraged capital, and more than 28,000 jobs created. Scaling is expensive. Scaling with the wrong legal identity makes it unnecessarily more expensive.
The Ghana Enterprises Agency (GEA), established under Act 1043, is the institutional home for MSME support in Ghana. Its objects are explicitly to “develop and implement national programmes aimed at encouraging and accelerating the growth of MSMEs” and to “strengthen the capacity and competitiveness of MSMEs”. But the support flows through classification. Under LI 2470, a micro enterprise is defined as having 1–5 employees and annual turnover below GH¢300,000; a small enterprise has 6–29 employees and turnover between GH¢300,000 and GH¢6 million.
Formalisation is the key that turns this classification into access. The GEA’s Business Advisory Centres and Business Resource Centres nationwide provide capacity building, access to funding, and eligibility for government- and donor-supported interventions, but the benefits of being a registered client are tied to formalisation. The BizBox Project, a partnership between GEA and the Mastercard Foundation, is targeting 250,000 young Ghanaians with training, start-up kits, and market linkages. An enterprise that has not registered its legal structure is not a participant in this framework. It is a spectator.
The government is the largest buyer in the country, with annual public procurement expenditure estimated at $3.5 billion, accounting for about 11 per cent of GDP. The Public Procurement Act, 2003 (Act 663) provides for margins of preference for domestic goods and works, and the government has proposed a margin of preference of about 30 per cent for Ghanaian goods. The Public Procurement Authority has also developed low-value and minor procurement guidelines specifically to bring MSMEs, artisans, and craftsmen into the formal procurement record.
But eligibility is not automatic. A business without a legal identity and proper registration cannot bid for contracts, cannot provide the documentation required for tender evaluation, and cannot claim the preference margins that the law allows. For a small manufacturer in Kumasi or a service provider in Tamale looking to move from local clients to institutional buyers, the right legal structure is not a marginal benefit. It is the price of admission to a market that is deliberately being opened to you.
If your scaling plan involves bringing in equity from an angel investor, a venture fund, or even a strategic partner, the legal structure is not a detail. It is the first thing a serious investor’s lawyer will examine. A sole proprietorship has no shares to issue. A general partnership under Act 152 can bring in partners but cannot issue equity shares. Investors overwhelmingly prefer Private Limited Companies, and the Companies Act, 2019 (Act 992) provides a clean framework for share issuance and transfer, a due diligence architecture, and the governance standards that external capital requires.
The VCTF’s entire model is built on this premise: it invests in Venture Capital Finance Companies that in turn invest equity and quasi-equity in SMEs, because the Fund recognises that high-cost debt alone has led to an “inordinately high business mortality rate” among SMEs. The Ghana Alternative Market (GAX), launched in 2013 with VCTF’s support, was specifically designed to give growth-oriented companies access to long-term capital. For a micro or small company with genuine scale ambitions, the question is not whether the compliance burden of a company structure is worth it. The question is whether you can afford to be invisible to the capital that will fund your next stage of growth.
A sole proprietorship dies with the proprietor. The ORC is explicit: the ownership of the business dies with the owner. A partnership dissolves when its partners change. A company under Act 992 enjoys perpetual succession: the entity continues to exist independently of its owners, and shares can be transferred without dismantling the business. This matters for scale in two concrete ways. First, it makes the business bankable and investable over a longer horizon; lenders and investors can underwrite an institution, not just a person. Second, it allows you to build a management team and a brand that is not inseparable from your own name. The ORC’s registration campaign across Ghana is built on this message: registration confers credibility, legal recognition, and the trust of customers and partners. Formalisation is a credibility signal, not just a compliance cost.
The final reason is cumulative. The Ghana Revenue Authority has introduced a Modified Taxation Scheme (MTS) for micro, small, and medium enterprises in the informal sector. Eligible taxpayers with annual incomes up to GHS 500,000 can pay a flat 3 per cent tax and register and pay via a dedicated mobile app, with options for fixed quarterly payments or turnover-based taxation. The GRA is even proposing to extend the MTS to qualifying small limited liability companies with annual turnover up to GH¢750,000, aligning the simplified regime with the VAT registration threshold.
This is the regulatory state actively building a bridge for small businesses to formalise without being crushed by compliance designed for large corporations. But the bridge leads into the formal system. An enterprise that has not registered its legal structure and obtained the necessary identification a TIN, an ORC registration, a place on the GEA client register cannot walk across it. The law and the regulatory architecture are not obstacles to scale. They are the operating system on which scale runs. The first step is deciding to stand on it.
The law does not require you to incorporate. It does not even require you to register as an MSME to trade. But the law draws a clear line between those within Ghana’s formal MSME framework and those outside it. Inside the line: limited liability under Act 992, priority access to the Collateral Registry and the VCTF ecosystem, eligibility for GEA programmes and BizBox, procurement preferences, investor readiness, perpetual succession, and the Modified Taxation Scheme. Outside the line: unlimited personal liability, invisible creditworthiness, and commercial contracts governed only by whatever bargaining power you can muster on your own.
For the micro and small entrepreneur in Ghana, the choice of legal structure is not a bureaucratic formality. It is the operating system on which every other scaling decision runs. The right structure will not make a bad business good. But the wrong structure will quietly cap a good business at the exact moment it is ready to grow. The law has built the ladder. The first step is deciding to stand on it.
Kweku Hammond, Snr Sales & Marketing Consultant/Faculty - Nova Business School Africa
